item.title: The Eye of the World
item.description: The first in the Wheel of Time series, the series famously finished by Brandon Sanderson, opens up a world that got me hooked from the first 10 chapters. Being the first of nearly 14 books, I figured this would be dense and full of set up. It definitely was, but it was a lot easier to follow than I initially thought. It doesn’t shy away from introducing elements that may or may not be expanded upon later, but from my perspective it wasn’t over the top. It was the right amount of world-building and foreshadowing.

item.title: The Great Hunt
item.description:
This rocked. Simple opening, but straight to the point. I liked this one a lot more than the first one, and felt like so much improved that it was totally worth the first one taking its time. I read a few reviews that not much happens in this one either; I slightly agree, but so much of what does happen is entertaining enough to excuse it.

We start right where we left off thankfully, with a small introduction to a character we never see again. This happens every now and then throughout the first book as well, but a few of those characters come back in this one and become more relevant (see Elayne and Min). I’m hoping the characters that didn’t get as much time in this one see the light of day in the next.

item.title: The Well of Ascension
item.description:
Oh Brandon, how far you’ve come. I took a small break between these to read Invisible Man, which I’m grateful for. It made me reflect on the parts of Mistborn I liked and disliked. I’m happy to say that this entry improved on the flaws of the first one- for the most part.

Vin and Elend make a decent couple. At first, they’re completely insufferable, with one complaining until it’s the others turn to do the same. Thankfully this is not the case for the entire book, but certainly the first half. To break this up, Sanderson finally gives us more character perspectives. These are so necessary, and start small but end up giving us great chapters. These aren’t common enough to push this into Stormlight territory, but it’s a much better attempt than the last.

item.title: Mistborn
item.description:
It seems like I read Sanderson’s works in the wrong order. So much of the ideas within this book seep into the Stormlight Archive, so much so it’s clear certain characters were frameworks for later characters. I don’t see that as a detriment, but it was difficult not to compare when the similarities are so glaring.

The story was good for the most part. While Kelsier takes on a lot of the bulk of the interesting and driving parts of the narrative, eventually the other main character, Vin, does grow into her own. Again, extremely difficult not to compare them directly to Kaladin and Shallan, when so much of their development and even story actions are similar if not the exact same. Honestly the more I write about it the more it bothers me, but during reading it didn’t too much so I’ll refrain from lowering the score more than I currently have it.

item.title: Wind and Truth
item.description:
Previously: Rhythm of War

I’m really torn on this one. Part of my loved this book, and part of me hated it. I gave it a 4 out of 5, so I must’ve liked it more than disliked; I still cannot get over the fact that it’s actually done. To be honest, a lot of the reason I gave it a 4 instead of anything lower is that there couldn’t possibly be the ending I know my heart wants. I want all of my favorite characters to come out not just good, but better, stronger (maybe even Kaladin/Shallan finally happening). Unfortunately, I am a realist.

item.title: Dawnshard
item.description:
Previous: Oathbringer

I’m not sure who keeps telling Brando Sando to keep making Novellas, but whoever it is needs to actually read them. I really can’t justify this being it’s own story. Even more than the first, this felt like a different type of filler. Filler with the audacity to be a hardcover.

My issues don’t come with the story at all really. I actually enjoyed Rysn, and thought every time she was on the page she felt real. She had valid concerns about being treated as a disabled person in a world not built for one. I loved these parts, and had never even considered before how impossible something like a wheelchair would be in a place without smooth paved roads. I even thought her ability to naturally lead her crew even though she was constantly anxious about it actually made sense. My issues come with how easily digestible this story is, and how it could’ve been condensed to take place in the interludes of Rhythm of War.

item.title: Edgedancer
item.description:
Previous: Words of Radiance

Definitely a novella that took me too long to finish, and not really because I was enjoying it. More so because I didn’t love Lift as a character. I was actually going to say I didn’t hate their childish behavior, but typing that out I had a gut feeling I wasn’t being honest with myself.

I really didn’t like how childish Lift was. Maybe that was her point, but I didn’t seem to grasp onto the story. Wendel, her spren, being a Squidward-type that doesn’t want to go anywhere or do anything was a nice contrast, but I couldn’t help feel sorry that we find out the character Wendel could have been with died in one of the earlier books, and was a more interesting character.

item.title: Oathbringer
item.description:
Holy Moly. What a ride. This book took FOREVER to finish. Exactly 3 months and a day to be exact. But it was so worth it.

A true continuation from Words of Radiance, this book follows the logical progression from where that book left off and really begins to open up the world. There are still lots of secrets left to unfold (Who is Wit? Who is the Cremling God that Lift meets in Edgedancer? What’s going to happen with Renarin? How is Odium going to exploit Taravangian? WHY DOESN’T KALADIN AND SHALLAN GET TOGETHER???) which has me very excited for the next two books.

item.title: Words of Radiance
item.description:
Modified: July 02 2024

I finished Words of Radiance two days ago, and it initially got a 4 out of 5. I loved the book. I really did, and was invested from start to finish.

It took me about 3 weeks (3 weeks and 3 days says Goodreads) and it really flew by. I enjoyed tackling such a huge tome of a novel.

The characters were awesome, even if I felt like the interlude characters could have been longer to make them a bit more memorable. I only remember maybe one of them, and it was Lift cause they had a really cool attitude and wanted to just eat some good food.
